item.title: Theoretical Foundations of Sequential Dynamic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2610.27449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many economic problems have several controls per period, whose joint choice is subject to the curse of dimensionality. Solving them in stages is computationally cheaper, but no general result says when staging is exact. I develop a separability theory, discrete choices and non-concave objectives included: staging is exact if utility, transitions, and constraints depend on earlier decisions only through a state passed forward. For each ordering the smallest such state exists and is unique up to relabeling. Any state that keeps staging exact for all preferences over later decisions and the future must carry everything the smallest one carries for the transition. For affine primitives, the smallest state consists of the linear combinations, such as cash-on-hand, on which later outcomes depend. Its dimensions pick the order whose largest stage is smallest. In a six-choice household model, each stage chooses one variable on a three-dimensional state, the joint problem all six.
item.dc:creator: Alan Lujan

item.title: Random Disclosure Costs: A Unified Theory of Disclosure
item.description: arXiv:2610.27627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a unified framework for a class of evidence games in which a sender, seeking to increase posterior expectations (e.g., a market price), chooses whether to reveal or withhold her information. Our model nests several classic models, including type-dependent disclosure costs or benefits, uncertain information endowment, and the market for lemons. Frictions are captured as random disclosure costs that are privately known to the sender and noisily inferred by the receiver. We derive a simple characterization of the equilibrium and show that it features increasing disclosure for lower frictions or greater fundamental uncertainty. Further, with high uncertainty or low frictions, greater uncertainty about disclosure costs decreases the likelihood of disclosure. Positive costs do not necessarily rule out unraveling to full disclosure, especially when outcomes have heavy tails or when disclosure costs are not constant. Finally, we demonstrate that the model can be estimated with a simple probit, suggesting that cost uncertainty is descriptive of real-world behavior.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Bertomeu, Edwige Cheynel, Keri Hu

item.title: Understanding CEO-Employee compensation dynamics: An agent-based simulation approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.27975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CEO compensation has often been examined from the top down, i.e., as the outcome of a negotiation between the CEO, the board of directors, and the shareholders. While these approaches have provided valuable insights into the nature of CEO compensation and its relations with firm performance and intra-firm inequality, we believe they leave aside the internal decision-making dynamics of CEOs and employees. To fill this research gap, we develop an agent-based model built on the NK framework in which a CEO compensated for long-term firm performance interacts with several employees rewarded for short-term departmental performance. This temporal dichotomy in their respective compensation functions creates a potential temporal misalignment of incentives. By varying the horizon considered by the CEO to make their decisions, we examine how this temporal (mis)alignment of incentives shapes firm performance and pay inequality between the CEO and the employees. Our findings suggest that aligning the CEO's horizon with the employees' short-term incentives yields the highest performance, raising both the level attained and the speed of improvement across all task environments examined. This finding contrasts with the usual advice given in CEO compensation research, which is to avoid short-termism. Furthermore, the model shows that the longest horizon examined produces both the lowest performance and the highest pay inequality. This pattern, commonly attributed to managerial power, emerges in our model from incentive misalignment alone, without agents holding any power over their own compensation.
item.dc:creator: Dar\'io Blanco-Fern\'andez

item.title: The Scale of Universalization in Multiplicative Kantian Equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2610.28180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplicative Kantian equilibrium requires agents to evaluate whether they would prefer all players to change their actions by a common proportional factor. This note argues that such a counterfactual is not fully specified by the material payoff environment alone: one must also specify the scale in which proportional universalization is performed. Building on the Sher-Roemer discussion of strategic non-invariance, we characterize how a smooth monotone reparametrization of actions changes the multiplicative Kantian first-order condition. We then illustrate the issue in a simple two-country abatement problem. Universalizing physical abatement and universalizing abatement expenditures are both natural interpretations of "doing one's part," but they lead to different Kantian outcomes, even though they describe the same material environment. The note also identifies special cases in which the interior first-order condition is representation-invariant, including common-exponent power transformations and symmetric profiles under identical transformations. The conclusion is constructive: applying multiplicative Kantian equilibrium to an economic environment requires specifying both the use of the Kantian criterion and the represented scale in which the Kantian counterfactual is evaluated.
item.dc:creator: Igor Sloev, Gerasimos Lianos

item.title: Entry, Exit, and Technological Progress in Markov-Perfect Duopoly
item.description: arXiv:2610.28440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes the existence and essential uniqueness of an intuitively refined Markov-perfect equilibrium in a duopoly game with sunk costs, barriers to entry, firm-specific technological progress, and irreversible exit. We develop an algorithm that quickly computes the equilibrium by solving for fixed points of a finite sequence of auxiliary contraction mappings, which we label Fake Backward Induction. We illustrate the game's practical value with a quantitative analysis of competition policy in a stochastically growing market with firms idiosyncratically learning by aging. Computing one equilibrium of this example takes 10.2 seconds on one Apple M5 Pro core.
item.dc:creator: Jaap H. Abbring, Jeffrey R. Campbell, Nan Yang

item.title: Overlapping Reserves without a Common Priority: Theory and an Application to School Choice in Chile
item.description: arXiv:2610.28471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study matching markets with overlapping reserves governed by heterogeneous priorities. When applicants qualify for multiple reserves, how they are routed can affect reserve utilization and which applicants are admitted. We introduce classify-and-rank choice rules that yield strategy-proof deferred acceptance mechanisms satisfying maximum reserve utilization and priority-respect. We axiomatically characterize our mechanism's admission outcomes for any given classification and reserve order. With two reserve categories, we provide a foundation for the reserve order and establish its distributional implications for access across eligibility groups. Using nine cycles of Chilean school admissions, which feature such reserves, we document reserve-utilization failures under the deployed mechanism and show that their frequency depends sharply on the reserve order. We show how our mechanism can be adapted to Chile's institutional setting to prevent such failures. Under this alternative mechanism, the reserve order generates a distributional pattern across eligibility groups, consistent with our theory.
item.dc:creator: Battal Do\u{g}an, Kenzo Imamura, M. Bumin Yenmez

item.title: Optimal Incentive-Compatible Assignments with Endogenous School Priorities
item.description: arXiv:2610.28582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study whether a planner can favor students at schools they rank more highly while preserving truthful reporting. The standard implementation of the deferred acceptance (DA) algorithm is typically not the solution. With interior cutoffs, DA with multiple tie-breaking (DA-MTB) solves the planner's optimization problem if and only if the planner's payoff from a school assignment is independent of the students' preferences. This is typically not the case, and strict incentive compatibility under DA-MTB leaves room for improvement via preference-dependent priority adjustments. We characterize optimal rank-dependent cutoff adjustments in a two-school model and show that, in a many-school environment, near-optimal approximately incentive-compatible assignments can be chosen with small support (so each type of student may only attend a small number of schools).
item.dc:creator: Federico Echenique, Juan S. Pereyra

item.title: Extending Mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2610.27839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given an incentive-compatible mechanism for a single agent on a restricted domain of valuations, we consider its incentive-compatible extensions to the entire valuation space. We identify two extreme extensions: the "keep-the-menu" extension, which minimizes buyer payoffs and maximizes canonical prices pointwise, and the "keep-the-pricing" extension, which maximizes buyer payoffs and minimizes canonical prices pointwise.
item.dc:creator: Sergiu Hart, Noam Nisan

item.title: Undergraduate Course Allocation through Competitive Markets
item.description: arXiv:2412.05691v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prevailing methods of course allocation at undergraduate institutions involve reserving seats to give priority to designated groups of students. We present a competitive equilibrium-based mechanism that assigns course seats using student preferences and course priorities. This mechanism satisfies approximate notions of stability, efficiency, envy-freeness, and strategy-proofness. We evaluate its performance relative to a mechanism widely used in practice using preferences estimated from university data. Our empirical findings demonstrate an improvement in student satisfaction and allocation fairness. The number of students who envy another student of weakly lower priority declines by 8 percentage points, or roughly 500 students.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kornbluth, Alexey Kushnir

item.title: On the existence of pure epsilon-equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2502.07585v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Departing from optimizing behavior by any $\epsilon>0$ ensures the existence of stable outcomes in a broad class of many-agent games where utilities are drawn from a joint distribution. Specifically, in a game with iid drawn utilities from a continuous distribution and any $\epsilon>0$, we show that as the number of agents gets large the probability that a pure $\epsilon$-equilibrium exists converges to 1, while, by contrast, the probability that a pure Nash equilibrium exists is known to converge to $1-1/e\approx 0.63$. The asymptotic existence of pure $\epsilon$-equilibrium extends to utilities that are negatively correlated across agents, and we identify a correlation threshold dependent on $\epsilon$ that is tight for the zero-sum case. We also study the cases of correlation across action profiles and of utility ties and, in all cases, we also characterize the asymptotic distribution of pure $\epsilon$-equilibria. Regarding pure Nash equilibrium---i.e., when $\epsilon=0$---our results nest, organize, and extend the existing literature. All our results and those from the prior literature are applications of our ``master theorem'', which builds on the Chen--Stein method and Stein's method.
item.dc:creator: Bary S. R. Pradelski, Bassel Tarbush

item.title: Collective decisions under uncertainty: efficiency, ex-ante fairness, and normalization
item.description: arXiv:2505.03232v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies preference aggregation under uncertainty in the multi-profile framework and characterizes a new class of aggregation rules that can address classical concerns about Harsanyi's (1995) utilitarian rules. Our aggregation rules, which we call \textit{relative fair aggregation rules}, are grounded in three key ideas: utilitarianism, egalitarianism, and the 0--1 normalization of individual utilities. These rules are parameterized by a set of weight vectors over individuals and evaluate each ambiguous alternative by taking the minimum weighted sum of 0--1 normalized utility levels over the weight set. For the characterization, we propose two novel axioms, \textit{weak preference for mixing} and \textit{restricted certainty independence}, with normative justifications. Additional results clarify how these axioms capture the utilitarian and egalitarian attitudes of the rules.
item.dc:creator: Leo Kurata, Kensei Nakamura

item.title: Disclosure under Noisy Information Processing
item.description: arXiv:2609.07898v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Capital markets process disclosures with noise. Adding this single friction overturns the standard characterization of costly voluntary disclosure. Firms may unravel to full disclosure despite strictly positive disclosure costs and, when unravelling fails, the model generically admits two equilibria rather than one. In the lower-threshold equilibrium, disclosure becomes more frequent as the cost rises and as reports become more accurate, falls with fundamental volatility when it is below the processing noise, but approaches full disclosure again when volatility grows large. These results help explain the mixed empirical evidence on the proprietary cost hypothesis and generate conditional predictions that distinguish high and low disclosure regimes. The model also explains why ESG ratings can be noisy, costly, and widely purchased, while still influencing market prices.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Bertomeu, Edwige Cheynel, Peicong Hu

item.title: Submission quotas as self-screening when manuscript production is cheap
item.description: arXiv:2610.04688v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI enables authors to produce more manuscripts at lower cost. But evaluation by expert editors and referees remains scarce. In this context, the value of an author's submission rights can increase. Major research repositories and journals are reacting by imposing submission quotas and fees. Non-transferable author quotas transform submission of a manuscript into a revealed-priority decision. Authors construct a portfolio of their highest-ranked manuscripts. A common fee charges an author for every manuscript they submit. Both methods have drawbacks. Quotas do not flexibly allocate scarce review capacity to authors who have unusually strong realised candidate sets. Fees can generate heterogeneous submission thresholds that may be systematically related to an author's baseline portfolio quality. In this paper, I derive the condition under which submission quotas yield weakly higher mean reviewed value than fees, given an equal expected review load. When project values are bounded and candidate manuscripts are abundant, an equal-load fee can price out some authors entirely.
item.dc:creator: Steve Lawford

item.title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2610.18625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Perez-Richet, Vasiliki Skreta

item.title: Matching Markets: Equilibrium Computation, Indivisible Goods, and Positional Externalities
item.description: arXiv:2109.14850v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Matching markets provide a mathematical framework for allocating scarce resources among strategic agents with heterogeneous preferences. While matching without money relies on ordinal stability and Pareto efficiency, Fisher and Arrow--Debreu markets mediate allocation through budgets and market-clearing prices. In this paper, we study the convex-analytic foundations, computational complexity, and external-utility extensions of Fisher matching markets. First, we formulate fractional resource allocation and linear Fisher markets via Fenchel conjugate duality and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Eisenberg--Gale convex program, showing how budget-weighted Nash social welfare characterizes competitive equilibria across linear and homothetic utility families. Second, we review topological existence via Sperner's lemma alongside polynomial-time combinatorial algorithms for divisible markets, including the Devanur--Papadimitriou--Saberi--Vazirani (DPSV) primal-dual max-flow algorithm and Orlin's strongly polynomial scaling algorithm. Third, we contrast the tractability of divisible markets with the $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness and $\mathsf{PPAD}$-completeness of indivisible Fisher markets and Competitive Equilibrium from Equal Incomes (CEEI), comparing $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibria, CEEI-FRAC, and Budish's Approximate CEEI mechanism. Finally, we analyze Fisher markets with positional (snob-effect) externalities, where buyer $i$'s utility for good $j$ scales with her relative share $(x_{ij}/\sum_{k} x_{kj})^{\alpha_i}$ for $\alpha_i > 0$. We prove that positional utility summands are convex on the nonnegative orthant, so utilitarian social welfare is maximized at exclusive corner allocations, whereas decentralized price-taking admits a unique budget-proportional equilibrium in single-good snob markets with a Price of Anarchy of $n^\alpha$ among $n$ symmetric buyers.
item.dc:creator: Bruce Changlong Xu, Andrew Yang, Ivan Villa-Renteria

item.title: Optimal Guarantees for Online Selection Over Time
item.description: arXiv:2408.11224v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prophet inequalities are a cornerstone in optimal stopping and online decision-making. Traditionally, they involve the sequential observation of $n$ non-negative independent random variables and face irrevocable accept-or-reject choices. The goal is to provide policies that provide a good competitive ratio against the optimal offline solution that can access all the values upfront---the so-called prophet value. In the \emph{prophet inequality over time problem} (POT), the decision-maker can commit to an accepted value for $\tau$ units of time, during which no new values can be accepted. This creates a trade-off between the duration of commitment and the opportunity to capture potentially higher future values. In this work, we provide best possible worst-case competitive ratios in the IID setting of POT for single-threshold algorithms and the optimal dynamic programming policy. We show a single-threshold algorithm that achieves a competitive ratio of $(1+e^{-2})/2\approx 0.567$, and we prove that no single-threshold algorithm can surpass this guarantee. With our techniques, we can analyze simple algorithms using $k$ thresholds and show that with $k=3$ it is possible to get a competitive ratio larger than $\approx 0.602$. Then, for each $n$, we prove it is possible to compute the tight worst-case competitive ratio of the optimal dynamic programming policy for instances with $n$ values by solving a convex optimization program. A limit analysis of the first-order optimality conditions yields a nonlinear differential equation showing that the optimal policy's asymptotic worst-case competitive ratio is $\approx 0.609$.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Perez-Salazar, Victor Verdugo
